prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The wind blew high, the waters raved, A ship drove on the land, A hundred human creatures saved Kneel’d down upon the sand. Three-score were drown’d, three-score were thrown Upon the black rocks wild, And thus among them, left alone, They found one helpless child. A seaman rough, to shipwreck bred, Stood out from all the rest, And gently laid the lonely head Upon his honest breast. And travelling o’er the desert wide It was a solemn joy, To see them, ever side by side, The sailor and the boy. In famine, sickness, hunger, thirst, The two were still but one, Until the strong man droop’d the first And felt his labours done. Then to a trusty friend he spake, “Across the desert wide, O take this poor boy for my sake!” And kiss’d the child and died. Toiling along in weary plight Through heavy jungle, mire, These two came later every night To warm them at the fire. Until the captain said one day, “O seaman good and kind, To save thyself now come away, And leave the boy behind!” The child was slumbering near the blaze: “O captain, let him rest Until it sinks, when God’s own ways Shall teach us what is best!” They watch’d the whiten’d ashy heap, They touch’d the child in vain; They did not leave him there asleep, He never woke again.

Driven by tempestuous winds and violent ocean swells, a vessel slammed into the shoreline. Exactly one hundred survivors dropped to their knees on the beach in gratitude for surviving the ordeal. Meanwhile, sixty individuals perished in the turbulent waters, and another sixty were cast against the dark, jagged reefs. Amidst the scattered group on the sand, a solitary, vulnerable young child was discovered without any family.

A veteran mariner, well-acquainted with nautical disasters, stepped forward from the crowd. He cradled the young child tenderly against his chest, adopting the role of his protector. 

As the group journeyed across a vast, barren wasteland, the bond between the rugged seafarer and the youngster was a deeply moving sight, for they remained constantly side by side. Even as starvation, disease, extreme hunger, and dehydration plagued the travellers, the duo faced every adversity as a single unit. However, the mighty sailor eventually lost his endurance and realized his life was coming to an end. Prior to drawing his final breath, he beseeched a dependable fellow traveller to look after the orphan for his sake, kissed the young boy goodbye, and expired.

The child and his new guardian continued the grueling trek, pushing through dense rainforests and deep mud. Every night, exhausted from their difficult plight, they arrived late to seek warmth around the campfire. 

Eventually, the expedition's captain urged the honorable seaman to abandon the youth to preserve his own life. The small child was sleeping peacefully beside the flames at that moment. The guardian refused to abandon him immediately, pleading with the commander to let the child rest undisturbed until the fire burned out, entrusting their ultimate fate to divine guidance.

Together, they watched the fire gradually die down into a pile of pale embers. When they reached out to wake the youth, he was completely unresponsive; he had passed away in his sleep, so they were spared from ever having to leave him behind.

Here is a complete, beautifully expanded narrative based on your bullet points:

***

The sea was merciless that night. A violent storm shattered the vessel against the jagged rocks of a wild, uncharted coast, leaving a small group of battered survivors stranded on the unforgiving shore. Among the wreckage sat a tiny, helpless boy—alone, frightened, and orphaned by the tempest. While most of the survivors were consumed by their own desperation to stay alive, a rough and weathered seaman, hardened by years of brutal tides, found his heart softened by the child’s tears. Driven by a sudden, fierce devotion, the sailor took the boy into his arms and vowed to keep him safe.

With no hope of immediate rescue, the survivors were forced to march inland across a vast and brutal desert. The trek was relentless under the scorching sun, but the seaman proved to be a faithful guardian. He carried the child across endless dunes, shielded him from the blistering heat, and willingly gave up his own meager rations so the boy would not go hungry. 

However, the merciless journey soon took a tragic toll. Famine and sickness swept through the dwindling party, and the seaman’s great strength finally began to fail him. Realizing his time was short, he summoned his most trusted friend to his side. With his final, shuddering breath, the dying sailor begged his companion to take up the mantle and protect the innocent boy. The friend gave his solemn word, and shortly after, the seaman passed away, leaving his legacy of love in the hands of another.

The journey only grew more perilous as the landscape shifted into jagged, freezing mountain passes. Resources dwindled to almost nothing, and the expedition’s captain, focused entirely on stark survival, pulled the friend aside. The captain urged him to abandon the boy, arguing that the child was a burden that would cost them all their lives. But the friend stood firm. Bound by his oath to the dead seaman and his own moral conviction, he refused to forsake the boy, choosing instead to carry the frail child through the bitter, punishing terrain.

That evening, the remaining travelers made camp against the howling wind. The friend wrapped the weary boy in his own coat and laid him down close to the warmth of the campfire. Throughout the dark hours, he watched over the child as the wood slowly burned down to glowing embers. 

In the quiet hours just before dawn, as the last embers of the fire flickered and died, the man gently reached out to wake the child. But the boy lay completely still. Softly, painlessly, and wrapped in the quiet comfort of sleep, the child had passed away—spared at last from the cruelty of the wasteland and the harshness of a world he was too fragile to endure.
outputs.L4:
The wooden hull of the *Northern Star* splintered against the jagged teeth of the black reef like tinder, her ribs snapped by the fury of a gale-driven sea. By dawn, the tempest had dragged the wreck into the deep, leaving behind only frozen wreckage washed ashore on a desolate, unnamed spit of northern wilderness. 

Out of the icy surf crawled Caleb, a veteran sailor with a face like carved oak, his skin cured by decades of brine and bitter winds. Behind him dragged Finnegan, his towering, quiet second mate, whose loyalty was as unyielding as the mountains looming over the coast. They were men of few words and hard habits, shaped by a life of brutal labor. But as the roar of the ocean receded, a feeble, thin cry pierced the silence of the snowbound shoreline.

Beneath the shelter of a overturned longboat, Caleb found the boy. He was no more than four years old, clutching the cold hand of a mother whom the frost had already claimed. The child was shivering violently, his cheeks flushed with a rising fever, his wide, blue eyes terrified and uncomprehending. 

Caleb did not hesitate. With calloused hands that had spent a lifetime hauling heavy hemp rope, he gently pried the boy from the mother’s dead embrace. He wrapped the child in his own dry, wool oilskin sweater, pressing the small, fragile body against his chest. 

"We walk, Finnegan," Caleb grunted, his voice like grinding stones. "There’s trappers fifty miles south over the ridge. We carry him."

Thus began an agonizing march into the white wilderness. The terrain was an unforgiving maze of razor-sharp slate, dense, snow-clogged pine forests, and frozen riverbeds. They had no food, no compass, and only the fading sun to guide them. 

As the days ground on, hunger became a gnawing beast inside them. The sickness that had gripped the boy worsened; his skin burned, and his breath came in ragged, wheezing rasps. Caleb and Finnegan took turns carrying him. Finnegan, despite his massive strength, began to falter first, his boots ruined and his toes blackened by frostbite. Yet, whenever it was his turn, the giant handled the sick child with an almost miraculous tenderness, humming low sea shanties to soothe the boy’s feverish nightmares.

On the fourth night, huddled in the shallow lee of a stone cliff during a howling blizzard, Finnegan quietly slipped away. He died in his sleep, his body curled defensively around the child to block the bitter wind. When Caleb awoke and found his companion cold and still, he offered no tears—the arctic air froze them before they could fall. He simply took Finnegan’s heavy coat, wrapped it around the boy, and hauled himself to his feet.

Now, Caleb was alone. His belly was a hollow pit, his legs felt carved of lead, and his lungs burned with every breath. Yet, looking down at the pale, frail child nestled against his chest, a profound, unfamiliar warmth ignited in the old sailor’s chest. He had spent his life running from the world, caring for nothing but the next tide. Now, this small, innocent soul was his entire universe. 

Through sheer, terrifying force of will, Caleb pressed on. He gave his last drops of melted snow to the boy. He stripped off his own gloves to warm the child’s freezing hands, feeling his own fingers turn numb and useless. Every step was an agonizing victory over death. "Nearly there, little mate," Caleb whispered through cracked, bleeding lips. "Just over the hill."

On the seventh day, the trees thinned. Caleb staggered onto a high, snow-draped ridge. Below, barely two miles away, thin wisps of grey smoke drifted from the chimneys of a logging settlement. Salvation was in sight. 

A breathless, choked laugh escaped Caleb’s throat. He sank to his knees in the deep snow, his body finally surrendering to total exhaustion. With trembling, clumsy hands, he pulled back the heavy layers of wool to tell the boy they had made it.

"Look, little mate," Caleb rasped. "We’re home."

But the boy did not look. 

The child’s face was smooth, peaceful, and terribly still. The fever was gone, replaced by the deep, unbroken quiet of the frost. The tiny heart beneath the wool had ceased its beating hours ago, surrendering quietly in the warmth of Caleb’s embrace while the sailor had blindly trudged forward.

Caleb stared at the small, motionless face. The world seemed to stop, the howling wind dropping to a dead, suffocating silence. The old sailor did not scream or curse the sky. Instead, a profound, tragic solemnity washed over him. He pulled the boy close once more, resting his chin upon the child’s golden hair.

Caleb knew he could not walk those final two miles. His oilskin was gone, his strength drained to the marrow, his heart shattered. He simply closed his eyes, wrapped his heavy, frozen arms tight around the child, and let the white quiet gather him in.

Weeks later, a hunting party from the settlement found them atop the ridge. They found the massive, frost-draped frame of the old sailor, curled like an impenetrable shield over the small child in his lap. Though mortality had claimed them both in the unforgiving wild, the men stood in awed silence before the sight—a testament to a dark world’s ultimate truth: that even in the face of inevitable tragedy, the human capacity for love and self-sacrifice shines with a light that death itself cannot extinguish.

Deep within the sanctuary of the whispering woods, **the** air grew cold and heavy with ancient magic. Shadows stretched across the mossy stone circle where **three** sacred monoliths stood, their worn surfaces glowing with faint, ethereal runes that had not been awakened for centuries.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a tragic narrative poem about a sailor who rescues an orphaned child from a shipwreck.
counterfactuals.output:
The black waves roared, the night was cold,
Of icy death the timbers told;
A shattered hull against the reef,
A night of thunder, rage, and grief.

Old Barnaby, with lantern bright,
Scanned the wild foam in dying light.
Amidst the splintered, drifting wood,
A lashed-down wooden cradle stood.

Inside, a babe with freezing breath
Was plucked from hungry jaws of death.
Beside the child, a pale hand hung,
To which the tiny fingers clung.

The mother slept beneath the swell;
He took the child he loved so well.
He wrapped her in his canvas vest,
And pressed the orphan to his chest.

He named her Mae, his morning star,
The brightest light in skies afar.
For seven years the sea was mild—
The grizzled tar and laughing child.

She learned the ropes, she knew the tides,
And sang where quiet water bides.
He was her father, teacher, guide,
And she his joy, his only pride.

But ocean carries dark deceit;
The black clouds gathered, cold and fleet.
A sudden gale, a squall of dread,
Turned gentle waves to crushing lead.

The mainmast cracked, the timber broke,
The wild abyss in fury spoke.
No rescue boat, no shelter nigh,
Beneath a dark, unforgiving sky.

He bound a beam of pine and oak,
And whispered softly as he spoke:
"Fear not, sweet Mae, you'll see the day,
Though I am carried far away."

He lashed her tight, he kissed her brow:
"The sea is harsh, but trust it now."
Then plunged into the freezing gray,
And kicked against the blinding spray.

With bleeding hands and gasping breath,
He fought the hungry tide of death,
And pushed her raft through churning foam,
To guide his little starlight home.

The timber grounded on the sand,
Safe on the dark and quiet land.
She called his name in frantic fear,
As through the surf his form drew near—

Washed up beside her, cold and still,
Beneath the shadow of the hill.
She pressed her face against his chest,
Where warmth had fled its wooden nest.

Twice pulled from depths where shadows sleep,
Twice orphaned by the cruel deep.
The morning rose in sullen gray,
To find her weeping by the bay.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

Upon a crest of golden dust,
The giant sailor lay.

"The tide is calling Old Man Jack..."

The boy placed stones upon his chest,
And wept into the land,

Beside the warming light;

Where wind and silence meet,

counterfactuals.prompt: Please write a 19th-century style poem about devotion, survival, and loss, featuring a sailor and a young boy facing harsh elements together.
counterfactuals.output:
The fury of the midnight sea
Had torn the battered hull apart;
Upon a small and leaking boat
The old man held the boy’s faint heart.
The gale blew shrieking from the north,
The salt-spray lashed like stinging sleet;
Yet through the wild and churning dark,
The old tar’s pulse was firm and fleet.

He stripped his oilskin, worn and frayed,
To wrap the shivering cabin-boy,
And drew him close against a chest
Where lived his last remaining joy.
"Hold fast, my lad," the sailor groaned,
"The morning star shall bring us grace;
Keep but thy young eyes fixed on mine,
And do not fear the tempest's face."

All through that grim, unyielding night,
They drifted on the black expanse;
No lighthouse threw its holy beam,
No mercy lit the gale’s wild dance.
The old man sang an ancient tune—
A lullaby of distant shores—
To drown the howling of the wind,
And rattle of the useless oars.

"I sleep, dear sir," the small voice fell,
As soft as foam upon the sand;
"The church bells ring... I hear them clear...
I feel my mother’s gentle hand."
The old tar pressed his frozen cheek
Against the boy's cold, marble brow;
He strove to pray, he strove to plead,
Before the dark abysses now.

The shivering ceased. The labored breath
Grew still beneath the shroud of snow;
The darkling waters whispered doom,
While solemn shadows swung below.
He held the stiff and lifeless form,
A blossom snapped by icy air,
Saved from the anger of the storm,
Yet dead within his desperate care.

When dawn broke grey in sullen lead
Across the endless, restless deep,
It found the living with the dead,
Where lonely tides their vigils keep.
No canvas spread, no harbor near,
No answer to his ragged moan—
Just one old heart that beat in grief,
Surviving on the waves, alone.

He folded tight the coat of wool,
And kissed the child upon the hair,
Then turned his eyes to meet the sun,
And offered up a final prayer:
That when his own weary watch was done,
And he was swept beneath the foam,
The boy would stand upon the quay,
To guide the old man safely home.

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you compose a poignant, old-fashioned narrative poem about a sea captain's crew rescuing a boy from black rocks, focusing on the ultimate sacrifice of the sailor who takes him in?
counterfactuals.output:
The salt-spray beat against the prow, the northern gales did roar,
Where jagged teeth of basalt sat off Scotland’s iron shore.
The captain stood upon the deck, his glass held to his eye,
And through the shroud of mist and foam, he heard a piteous cry.

"Avast!" the watchful captain called, "Bring her about the wind!
There’s life upon the undertow, though hopeless 'tis to find!"
For pinned upon the midnight stone, where white waves whipped to froth,
There clung a tiny, shivering boy against the ocean's wrath.

No wreck was seen, no timber drifted—only sea and spray,
A starveling child upon the rocks, snatched from the jaws of day.
Old Silas was a quiet tar, who’d lost his own at sea,
With hands like iron, eyes like slate, as stern as wind could be.

Yet Silas leapt into the skiff through breakers cold and black,
He fought the fury of the tide, and brought the urchin back.
They wrapped the boy in woolen fleece beside the galley fire,
While Silas held him in his arms as winds rose ever higher.

"You've found a home, my little lad," the weathered sailor swore,
"No wave shall take thee from my side, nor cast thee to the shore."
And from that night, the child became the old man’s light and grace,
A bloom of sun upon the deck, a smile upon his face.

He taught the boy to bind the hemp, to read the stars by night,
To know the secrets of the wind, and hold the tiller tight.
A father’s love, so long entombed beneath the salty brine,
Awoke within the boatswain’s chest—a mercy half-divine.

Three winters passed in calm and storm, until that fateful dawn,
When off the crags of Cape Defiance, a monstrous gale was born.
The sky turned black as iron ore, the sea raised up its head,
And hurled the ship through screaming gullys, churning up the dead.

A wall of water, thick and green, roared down the mainmast tall,
It swept the deck with icy rage to drown us one and all.
The boy was pinned against the rail, the ocean stretched its hand,
To drag him down to fathomless dark, far from the sight of land.

And with the wave, a broken spar came crashing through the shroud,
A heavy beam of splintered oak, beneath the thunder-cloud.
It fell toward the helpless child—but Silas saw the blow,
And leapt between the strike of death and him he cherished so.

The timbers struck with terrible force; the old man took the stroke,
He shielded with his aging frame the lad before he broke.
He tossed the boy to safe shelter, clear of the surging foam,
Just as the black wave crushed his chest and claimed the sailor home.

When swept the tempest from the deck and calm restored the sky,
We laid Old Silas on the hatch, to watch his body die.
The boy was weeping at his side, and held his calloused hand,
Which now grew cold as winter ice upon a barren strand.

"Weep not, my son," Old Silas breathed, his voice a fading breeze,
"I kept thee from the black rock's teeth, I save thee from the seas.
My tide is out, my course is run, the harbour lights are clear...
I go to sleep beneath the deep, with nothing left to fear."

They sewed him in his canvas shroud, with iron at his feet,
And cast him to the abyss below, where wave and heavens meet.
The boy grew up to master ships, through every gale and tide,
And carried still the sailor’s love, for which Old Silas died.
